Mentorship · Part 4

Stop Hoping. Start Building - Part 4

The Cold Email That Turns a Foreign Professor Who is a Stranger Into a Sponsor

By Raphael OnukuSeptember 10, 20269 minute read

Mentorship

← All writing

Cold emails are one of those things people hear about, but they rarely understand why it works or how to do it properly. When you come from a place where most opportunities look like luck, it is easy to assume that emailing a professor is just another form of begging. But the truth is simpler and more empowering: in many countries, contacting a professor directly is part of the normal system, not a desperate shortcut. It is a professional way to enter the conversation early, before you become just another name inside a pile of applications.

This approach shows up strongly in places like Asia, Australia, Canada, and some research routes across Europe, because the PhD is often tied to a lab, a project, or a professor’s funding. In those systems, the professor is not only supervising your work, the professor may also be the person deciding whether there is money, space, and a real research need that you can fill. Even in the U.S., where many programs admit you first and match you later through rotations, a cold email can still work when a PI has funding and is actively looking for someone with a particular skill set. It is not the only path, but it is a real path.

So I want you to reframe the cold email from the start. A cold email is not you asking for mercy. A cold email is you making a case for fit. You are saying, “This is who I am, this is what I am building toward, this is why your lab makes sense for that path, and this is what I can contribute.” That is a different energy entirely, and when it is done well, it reads like a future colleague introducing themselves, not a random person sending a long story.

The reason many people fail at this is that they rush the email. They want to email twenty professors in one day, so they write one generic message and copy paste it everywhere. Professors can smell that from the first two lines. The first job of a cold email is not to impress. The first job is to prove that you are intentional, and intentional people do not send generic messages.

That intentionality starts before you even open your email draft. I always advise people to begin with the professor’s university profile, not just Google Scholar. University profiles often reveal what the lab is focused on right now, and sometimes that focus has shifted since the professor moved institutions. I experienced this in a very real way: my current PhD professor had a deep history in fungi research, but after joining my university a few years ago, he drifted strongly into peptide research. Imagine how it would be if I wrote my cold email based only on the older identity (assuming cold email is required), my message would have sounded like I did not know what the lab had become.

After the profile, I go into the work. Not one abstract, not one random paper, but a serious read of the professor’s recent output. I usually aim for six to nine relevant papers, not because I want to mention all of them in the email, but because I want to understand the lab’s direction, the methods they actually use, the questions they keep repeating, and the problems they are trying to solve. When you read that many, patterns start to appear, and those patterns give you the strongest lines in your email. You stop sounding like a fan and start sounding like someone who understands the work.

There is another layer that makes cold emails stronger, and most applicants ignore it. Sometimes the smartest move is to speak to current or past lab members before you even email the PI. A quick respectful message to a graduate student or postdoc can reveal how the lab is structured, what the PI values, and what kind of student succeeds there. And sometimes you get lucky in the best way, because some labs empower senior students and postdocs to help screen or recruit people who fit the lab’s needs. One good conversation can turn your cold email from a shot in the dark into a warm introduction, even if the PI does not know you yet.

Once you have done that groundwork, the email becomes easier to write because you are not guessing. You already know what you are connecting to. At that point, the cold email is simply a clean bridge between their work and your preparation. It should be short enough that the PI can read it on a busy day, but specific enough that it does not look like you emailed ten other professors that morning.

Timing also matters. I do not treat cold emails like WhatsApp chat where I send whenever I remember. I treat it like professional communication. I often schedule my emails to land between 8:30 and 10:00 AM in the recipient’s local time because many professors scan emails around that period before meetings and lab work swallow the day. It does not guarantee a response, but it increases the chance that your email is seen when their mind is still fresh, not when they are already drowning.

Your email identity matters more than people think. If you have an institutional email address, use it, because it signals legitimacy and reduces friction. If you do not, you must still look professional, and that starts with your email address. Something like blessedqueen4eva@gmail.com or bigmanmoney2020@gmail.com may be personal and fun, but it creates doubt before your message is even read. A clean option like firstname.lastname@gmail.com, firstinitiallastname@gmail.com, or lastname.firstname@gmail.com is simple and serious, and it helps you enter the space with respect.

Now let us talk about attachments, because this is where many people also underperform. A PI cannot evaluate you properly if everything is only claims inside an email. This is why I attach supporting documents early, especially a well prepared CV. In my own case, when I was sending cold emails to a professor at the University of Queensland in Australia during my 2023 cycle, I attached my CV and transcripts because I wanted the professor to assess my readiness without unnecessary back and forth. When you attach documents, name them cleanly, not “final_final_revised_cv.pdf,” and do not attach five random files that overwhelm the reader. By the way, that was my first PhD admission offer, but I chose the US instead.

When the email itself is being drafted, I keep it anchored on four simple moves that flow naturally. I introduce myself in one clear line. I show specific awareness of the lab’s current work in a way that proves I did the reading. I connect that work to my own preparation and interests, using evidence, not hype. Then I make a clear request, usually whether they are accepting students and whether we can have a brief meeting or call.

Here is what a true cold email can look like in real life. You can copy the structure, but you must rewrite the content so it sounds like you and reflects the professor you are contacting.

Subject: Prospective MSc/PhD applicant interested in joining your lab (Fall 2027)

Dear Professor [Last Name],

My name is [Your Name], and I am a [final year student or graduate] in [Your Program] at [Your University] with a strong interest in [your field]. I am reaching out because your work on [specific theme from their recent work] closely matches the direction I am building toward.

I recently read your recent papers on [paper topic 1] and [paper topic 2], and I was especially interested in how your group is approaching [specific method, finding, or problem]. My background includes [one or two relevant experiences], and I have developed skills in [two or three skills that match their lab], which I believe could contribute to your ongoing work in [lab’s current direction].

I plan to apply for [MSc/PhD] in [term and year], and I wanted to ask if you are currently accepting graduate students and whether there may be opportunities for funding in your group. If you are open to it, I would appreciate a brief call at your convenience to learn whether my interests align with your current priorities. I have attached my CV and transcript for your review.

Thank you for your time, and I look forward to hearing from you.

Sincerely,

[Your Full Name]

[Current University or City, Country]

After you send the email, the next test is emotional discipline. Many people send a cold email today and start checking their inbox every hour, and after two days they conclude the professor does not like them. That is not how academia works. Professors travel, teach, review papers, write grants, manage lab issues, and sometimes they simply forget to reply even when they intended to. Silence is not always rejection, and panic is never strategy.

This is why I recommend patience with structure. I give it two to four weeks before I send a reminder, and during that waiting period I keep building other options. I do not pause my whole future because I am waiting for one professor. That is how people get stuck. If the reply comes, beautiful. If it does not, you still have momentum.

When it is time to follow up, the reminder must be shorter and calmer than the first email. It should not guilt trip the professor. It should not sound like anger disguised as politeness. It should simply refresh their memory and give them an easy path to respond, even if their response is just a yes or no.

Here is a reminder email that works without sounding needy or aggressive.

Subject: Follow up on prospective graduate student inquiry

Dear Professor [Last Name],

I hope this email finds you well.

I wanted to follow up on my email from [date] regarding potential opportunities to join your lab as a prospective [MSc/PhD] student. I remain very interested in your group’s work on [specific theme], and I would be grateful to know if you might be accepting new students for [term and year].I understand you may be busy, so a brief reply whenever convenient would be greatly appreciated. Thank you again for your time.

Sincerely,

[Your Full Name]

If you send that reminder and still get no response, you move on without drama. This is where many people damage their own reputation by sending multiple follow ups, emotional messages, or long paragraphs trying to force a reply. Do not do that. Sometimes the professor will still respond later, and when that happens, you receive it on their terms and continue the conversation professionally. But your job is to keep your pipeline moving, because the goal is not to win one professor’s attention, the goal is to secure a real opportunity.

Cold emailing works when you treat it like a system, not a miracle. You research deeply, you write like a professional, you send at sensible times, you attach real evidence, you follow up with patience, and you keep building options. That is the kind of approach that quietly separates people who keep dreaming from people who start getting replies, meetings, and funded offers.
